name: DeepMOT (Xu et al., CVPR 2020) and GMTracker learnable graph matching (He et al., CVPR 2021) - training association features through a differentiable assignment
bibliography: [S1] Yihong Xu, Aljosa Osep, Yutong Ban, Radu Horaud, Laura Leal-Taixe, Xavier Alameda-Pineda. 'How To Train Your Deep Multi-Object Tracker'. CVPR 2020, pp. 6787-6796. arXiv:1906.06618 v3 (23 Apr 2020), https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.06618 (PDF read: https://arxiv.org/pdf/1906.06618). Earlier arXiv versions v1/v2 (2019) were titled 'DeepMOT: A Differentiable Framework for Training Multiple Object Trackers' (the older code headers still use that title). These are the same work, not independent. CVF DOI 10.1109/CVPR42600.2020.00682 [uncertain]. Official code: (a) https://github.com/yihongXU/deepMOT. On branch master there is only a README that points to GitLab. Branch 'obsolete' holds the earlier SiamRPN/GOTURN MOT-by-SOT training code (models/DHN.py, utils/loss.py, train_mot.py). (b) https://gitlab.inria.fr/robotlearn/deepmot holds the CVPR release: train_DHN/, train_tracktor/ (DeepMOT-Tracktor training), test_tracktor/. LGPL-3.0. Pretrained DHN.pth and DeepMOT-Tracktor.pth are on Google Drive (not downloaded). [S2] Jiawei He, Zehao Huang, Naiyan Wang, Zhaoxiang Zhang (CASIA / UCAS / TuSimple, Chinese authors). 'Learnable Graph Matching: Incorporating Graph Partitioning with Deep Feature Learning for Multiple Object Tracking'. CVPR 2021, pp. 5299-5309 [uncertain page range]. arXiv:2103.16178 v1 (30 Mar 2021), https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.16178. Official code: https://github.com/jiaweihe1996/GMTracker (last push 2021-12-31). It bundles a modified qpth (OptNet QP layer). [S3, duplicate/extension, NOT independent] Same four authors, 'Learnable Graph Matching: A Practical Paradigm for Data Association', arXiv:2303.15414 (v1 Mar 2023, v2 Feb 2024), https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.15414. It is a journal-style extension (venue not stated on the arXiv page [uncertain]). It repeats the MOT17-val ablations of S2 and adds MOT20, a GST solver speed-up, ScanNet image matching and 3DMatch registration. Its numbers on MOT17 val are the same experiments as S2, not a replication. Related methods mentioned only as alternatives, not analysed in depth: OptNet (Amos & Kolter, ICML 2017), the source of S2's implicit-gradient QP layer; Sinkhorn/dustbin matching and blackbox differentiation of combinatorial solvers (Vlastelica et al., ICLR 2020), both recommended below instead of DHN [not opened in this item].

inputs_state_output: DeepMOT [S1]. Inputs: RGB frames and the previous boxes of the tracks. The tracker is Tracktor (Faster R-CNN FPN-ResNet101 regression head) or a SOT (SiamRPN, GOTURN). State: one box per track. With +ReIDhead, the track embedding is the mean of a 128-d FC ReID head (about 131K params) over the last 10 frames. Output: regressed boxes per track (plus embeddings). The Deep Hungarian Net (DHN) is NOT part of the tracker at inference. It is a frozen, pre-trained network (2-layer bidirectional GRU, hidden 256, row-wise then column-wise flattening, 3 FC layers that in the released code have no nonlinearity between them, then a sigmoid). Its input is a tracks x ground-truth distance matrix D = (normalised centre distance + (1 - IoU)) / 2. In the ReID version a second D is built as 0.5*(1 - cos) between track embeddings and ReID embeddings of the GT boxes. Its output is a soft assignment A~ in [0,1]^{N x M} that exists only to carry gradients from the loss. GMTracker [S2]. Inputs: public detections refined by Tracktor (or CenterTrack detections), with 512-d ReID features from a frozen ResNet-50 pretrained on Market1501/Duke/CUHK03, plus 2 trainable FC layers (512). Tracklet state: the mean of all past appearance features of the tracklet (the code also computes a moving average) and a Kalman-filter-predicted box with ECC camera-motion compensation. A cross-graph GCN (one layer) uses weights cos + IoU. The IoU is used only for static-camera videos; for moving-camera videos only appearance is used. Detection-graph and tracklet-graph edge features are l2([h_i, h_i']). Output: a relaxed QP matching score map X (nd x nt), sharpened by a softmax with temperature 1e-3 (code: 'voting layer', alpha 1000), then greedy rounding at inference. Comparison with ours: our per-(track, real region) input is 68 regional FlyVis activity features, an observed-target descriptor, 8 geometry inputs and 6 assignment-context features. The state is FlyVis recurrent state over exemplar and search frames, plus a ridge target model fitted on 4 exemplar frames. GMTracker's vertex affinity B_ij = cos(h_i, h_j) is the closest analogue of our per-action score. The key difference: GMTracker feeds this affinity into the solver used at inference. We feed our score only into a gated box transfer, and the native ByteTrack solver then runs on (1 - IoU) fused with detection confidence (tracking/xywh_bytetrack.py; fuse_score=True on the first association; linear_assignment with match_thresh 0.8). Neither source has a recurrent spatial map comparable to FlyVis. Their 'state' is a pooled embedding plus a box, i.e. as pooled as our 68 regional features.
action_and_refusal: DeepMOT. At inference the learned parts change box regression and appearance only. Association, births and deaths use non-learned Tracktor track management: regression, classification-score kill, public-detection births, ReID of inactive tracks. Refusal is thus purely hand-set thresholds. Inside the loss, 'no match' is a dustbin. A constant column (for FP) and a constant row (for FN) with value delta are appended to A~ before a row-wise or column-wise softmax with a scale factor. delta = 0.5 with scale 100 in the Tracktor release; the obsolete SiamRPN code defaults to 0.7 and smax_scale 10. Structurally this is the same as our fixed no-action logit 0 competing in a softmax with the action scores. The difference is that in DeepMOT the dustbin belongs to the evaluator's matching (counting FP/FN), not to the tracker's decision. GMTracker. Action = the association itself, read off the QP score map by greedy rounding. Refusal is hand-set and applied after the solver: a match is deleted if IoU = 0, if the Kalman Mahalanobis gate exceeds 9.4877 (chi2 0.95), or if the appearance cosine is below sigma (0.6 moving camera, 0.7 static). An IoU-Hungarian fallback (IoU >= 0.3) then runs on the leftovers. The appendix (Fig. A) names sigma as the most sensitive hyperparameter. Training never contains an explicit 'unmatched / new' option. The code drops every current-frame detection whose GT identity is not among the tracklets, and the QP inequality only lets tracklet rows sum to <= 1. Compared with ours: we have an explicit 'unmatched' action and a fixed logit-0 baseline with a probability threshold chosen on 20 videos. Neither source learns when to keep the default decision. Both put abstention into constants and thresholds, as we do. Neither offers a better-founded abstention mechanism.
labels_and_loss: DeepMOT. (1) DHN training. 114,483 training and 17,880 test (D, A) matrix pairs built from MOT15-17 GT boxes vs public detections. Augmentation: entries above a random uniform threshold are set to a large value. Labels come from the Hungarian algorithm (the CLEAR-MOT variant). Loss: weighted binary focal loss (gamma 2) with weight w0 = n1/(n0+n1) for the dominant zero class, scaled x10 in the code. RMSprop, lr 3e-4, 20 epochs. Then the DHN is frozen. (2) Tracker training. Pairs of consecutive frames are sampled (10 consecutive frames for the ReID head). Tracks are initialised from GT boxes with perturbation: scale 0.8-1.2, shift up to 0.25 of w/h, each applied with probability 0.4 in the Tracktor code. The forward pass predicts t+1 boxes, D is built against the GT, and A~ = DHN(D). Loss = delta_balance*(1 - dMOTA) + lambda*(1 - dMOTP) with dMOTA = 1 - (FP~ + FN~ + gamma*IDS~)/M. FP~/FN~ are the sums of the dustbin column/row after softmax. IDS~ sums column-softmax mass on tracks other than the one matched to the same GT in the previous frame. dMOTP is the mean distance of matched pairs under a binary TP mask (paper: delta 0.5, lambda 5, gamma 2). Code-level details that matter: (a) the TP mask for dMOTP is a hard argmax (detached), so dMOTP's gradient flows through D only, not through the assignment. (b) In the Tracktor release the geometric branch uses mota = (FN~ + FP~)/M, and IDS (weight 2) is applied only on the appearance-distance branch: loss = 5*motp + mota + 5*motp_app + mota_app. (c) Only RCNN_bbox_pred and reid_branch are trainable (Adam lr 1e-4), with BatchNorm frozen. (d) The SiamRPN code adds a 10x focal classification loss on anchors (IoU > 0.6 positive, < 0.3 negative), which is not in the paper's Eq. 9. Class imbalance in the tracker loss is not handled beyond the dustbin. Labels are evaluator-style GT matching, NOT the consequence of the tracker's own decisions. GMTracker. Labels: y_ij = 1 iff detection i and tracklet j share a GT identity. Training graphs are built entirely from GT tracks: npytrain_gt plus gt.txt filtered to visible pedestrians, classes 1-2, visibility >= 0.2. Tracklets with no update within MAXAGE 100 are dropped, and detections with no matching tracklet are removed. So every training detection is matchable and there are no false positives or births. Loss (paper Eq. 14): weighted BCE with positive weight k = nt - 1, applied to the temperature-softmaxed score. Code: nn.BCELoss with class-balanced weights computed per graph. Adam, lr 1e-5 in config.py (the paper says 5e-5 [uncertain which was used]), weight decay 1e-5, cosine schedule, 2 epochs, batch 1. NaN gradients are skipped. Neutral or rare positive events are not modelled. Both sources label pairwise identity correctness. Ours labels the measured good/neutral/harm consequence of transferring a box relative to the baseline assignment, which is closer to decision consequences than either source.
data_camera_resolution_rate: DeepMOT. Pedestrian MOT15/16/17 only. Ablation split: each MOT17 train sequence is cut in time: first 50% for training, last 25% for validation. Train: 2,664 frames, 35,836 GT boxes, 306 identities. Val: 1,328 frames, 200 identities. Train and validation therefore come from the SAME 7 sequences (not independent videos). Benchmark models are trained on the full MOT17 train set and tested on the MOTChallenge servers, averaged over DPM/SDP/FRCNN public detections. Mixed static and moving cameras; Tracktor uses ECC camera-motion compensation in training and inference. MOT17 resolution is mostly 1920x1080 (one sequence at 640x480), 14-30 fps. Initial conditions: GT-box initialisation with random perturbation. GMTracker. MOT16/17 (S3 adds MOT20). Ablations use 3-fold cross-validation over the 7 MOT17 train sequences, following MPNTrack. The released config has one fold with val sequences MOT17-04 and MOT17-11. Static vs moving camera is handled with different thresholds and the GCN geometry term is off for moving cameras. Kalman filter + ECC motion. Max age 100 frames (Table 4 shows longer ages help graph matching more than Hungarian). One dataloader branch samples only frames with index mod 5 = 3 [uncertain under which setting]. Training uses GT boxes and GT tracklets; testing uses Tracktor-refined public detections. Compared with BDD100K MOT (our bench): we have many independent driving videos with strong ego-motion, night/glare conditions and multiple classes. Our split is fit20/fit84/eval26 by video. Neither source evaluated on BDD100K or on independent-video splits for its ablations.

distinguishing_ablations: Ablations that isolate the assignment-aware loss from the features. (1) DeepMOT Table 2: the same architecture trained with Smooth L1 box regression (a per-target loss after a non-differentiable Hungarian match to GT) vs the DeepMOT loss. MOTA 60.38 vs 60.66 (+0.28), IDF1 71.27 vs 72.32, IDS 164 vs 118, FP 294 vs 218. Removing the IDS term raises IDS from 118 to 124. dMOTA alone lowers MOTP to 88.31 (below Vanilla 89.50). (2) DeepMOT Table 3: DeepMOT vs Smooth L1 on GOTURN (+1.81 MOTA) and SiamRPN (+0.65 MOTA). The larger gains in Table 3/4 come from fine-tuning on video at all (pre-trained to Smooth L1: +6.29 GOTURN), not from the assignment-aware loss. (3) GMTracker Table 2 is the cleanest isolation. With the same inference (graph-matching QP), training the features THROUGH the QP layer vs training them without it gives IDF1 71.5 vs 70.2 (+1.3), MOTA unchanged at 62.3. Inference with GM vs Hungarian on features trained without GM gives 70.2 vs 69.5 (+0.7). (4) GMTracker Table 1: graph matching with frozen, untrained features already gives +1.9 IDF1 over Hungarian (70.0 vs 68.1). That is an inference-time second-order (neighbour-relation) effect, not a training effect. Learned feature refinement adds only +0.4 to +0.6. Negative results and limitations. DeepMOT on MOT15 test gives no MOTA gain (44.1 = 44.1), lower IDF1 (46.0 vs 46.7) and more IDS (1347 vs 1318); the authors attribute this to noisy labels. On MOT17 test, MOTP is LOWER than vanilla Tracktor (77.2 vs 78.0) despite the dMOTP term. The authors call the near-zero IDS effect of the Base variant 'surprising': the loss could not reduce IDS until a trainable ReID head was added. The DHN is only an approximation: about 7% weighted error, many missing assignments (12-13%) on matrices seen during training, worse on large matrices. So the 'differentiable MOTA' is a biased surrogate. GMTracker: MOTA is unaffected by the matching layer. The QP is O(nd^3 nt^3) and very slow (S3: 8861 s solver time on MOT17 val before GST). The sigma threshold is the most sensitive hyperparameter. Training used GT boxes only. Inference adds k-reciprocal re-ranking of the vertex affinity (gmatching.py: Mp = 1 - re_ranking(...)), which is not described in the paper, so the reported inference is not exactly the trained objective. Runs/seeds: none of the tables report repeated runs, seeds, variance or confidence intervals. DeepMOT's val split shares sequences with training. Mandatory components for the claimed effect: in DeepMOT, a trainable identity component (ReID head) is needed for the IDS term to matter (Table 1). In GMTracker, the solver must be present in both training and inference to get the full +2.0 IDF1 (Table 2), and geometry adds about 0.9-1.0.
explanations_addressed: (1) Lost discriminative/spatial information in the readout. CAUTION / indirect. In both sources the useful signal comes from strong appearance embeddings: a 25M-param external ReID, a 131K ReID head, or a frozen ResNet-50 ReID with trainable FC. GMTracker's training-through-solver gain (+1.3 IDF1) sits on top of an already discriminative ReID. Neither source shows that an assignment-aware loss can recover information that the features do not contain. No evidence on pooled vs spatial maps. (2) Target-vs-neighbour identification. DESIGN ANALOGY, fairly strong. GMTracker's second-order edges compare the relation of a tracklet to its neighbours with the relation of a detection to its neighbours (edge features l2([h_i, h_i'])). That alone gives +1.9 IDF1 with frozen features (Table 1), and it degrades less with long max age (Table 4). Our 6 context features (own cost, best competing track cost, best alternative detection cost, margin, flags) are a scalar, first-order version of this. A pairwise target-neighbour relation feature computed from FlyVis activity would be the analogue. (3) Training objective mismatched to the final assignment. DIRECT EVIDENCE in their settings, with small effects. DeepMOT Table 2: loss through a soft assignment vs Smooth L1 gives +0.28 MOTA, -46 IDS. GMTracker Table 2: training through the inference solver gives +1.3 IDF1. Both are single runs without CIs on MOTChallenge pedestrians. This is the explanation the item asks about. It supports trying a decision-consistent loss, but the expected magnitude is modest. (4) Rare useful events with high harm cost. NOT ADDRESSED. Both treat matching as balanced pairwise classification: focal-loss class weights for DHN, k = nt - 1 positive weight in GMTracker, and an IDS weight gamma = 2 in DeepMOT. Neither models rare beneficial overrides of a default decision or asymmetric harm. (5) Insufficient history. DIRECT, limited. GMTracker Table 3: averaging the tracklet appearance over all past detections vs the last frame gives +0.9 IDF1, and max age 100-150 helps graph matching (Table 4). DeepMOT averages ReID over the last 10 frames by design. This is consistent with our temporal audit (only 14,252 of 37,296 queries have a prior query with supported regions), but it does not tell us how to supply missing history. (6) Limits of the action. DESIGN ANALOGY / caution. GMTracker's oracle-association gap (Table A: 71.5 vs 77.2 IDF1, IDS 1017 vs 14) is the analogue of our oracle reserve (+5.24 pp full boxes in eye, +7.25 whole frame). Neither source changes what the action can reach. DeepMOT only changes box regression and embeddings, not the action set.
evidence_strength: Both are peer-reviewed CVPR papers with official code. I verified that the code exists and that its training/inference files implement the described losses, with the noted discrepancies. I did not run it. The GMTracker extension (S3) is by the same authors on the same experiments, so it is not an independent confirmation. I found no independent replication of either ablation during this check [uncertain: not searched exhaustively]. Overall strength: MODERATE that differentiable assignment surrogates are feasible and give consistent but small gains on pedestrian MOT. WEAK for the specific claim that an assignment-aware loss beats a per-pair or per-target loss by a margin relevant to us. Reasons: single runs, no seeds or CIs, DeepMOT validation drawn from the same sequences as training, differences of 0.1-0.3 MOTA, and one +1.3 IDF1 isolation in GMTracker trained on GT boxes only.
difference_from_tried: What is genuinely new compared with what we tried: training the readout THROUGH a smooth surrogate of the solver used at inference, so that the loss is the frame-level association outcome. Our heads were per-action MSE regression of each score to {-1,0,+1}, followed by a separately calibrated softmax-plus-threshold policy. That is a two-stage objective. Training never sees the decision rule (softmax with the fixed logit 0 and the threshold). It never sees interactions between several tracks acting in the same frame, or between a transferred box and competing tracks' costs. DeepMOT's dustbin softmax (constant delta column) is structurally identical to our fixed baseline logit 0. The difference is that DeepMOT backpropagates through it, while we calibrate a threshold afterwards. What is NOT new: our labels already encode decision consequences more faithfully than either source. We replay the native ByteTrack association with each action and label good/neutral/harm against GT identity, while both sources use evaluator-style GT pair matching. For single, mutually exclusive actions with exact enumerated outcomes, a differentiable Hungarian surrogate adds nothing over directly maximising the expected outcome under the softmax policy, sum_a p_a * y_a with p_baseline fixed by logit 0. That is a listwise or counterfactual policy loss, close to item A02. The surrogate adds value only for joint, multi-track effects inside one frame, or for continuous actions (a soft box), where the outcome cannot be enumerated per action. GMTracker's second-order neighbour-relation features differ from our scalar context features and are the other new element. The fixed and learned 3-peak association (KeepTrack-style) and category replacement were all first-order per-candidate scorers. None compared target-neighbour relations.
candidate_node_change: Node: the readout ('считывание активности') and its training objective. The FlyVis core, connections and parameters stay unchanged; the 68 regional features, descriptor, geometry and context stay as inputs. Change A (decision-consistent loss, cheapest): replace per-action MSE with an expected-outcome softmax loss over {baseline logit 0, unmatched, the actions of this query}. L = -sum_a softmax(s)_a * y_a + beta * sum_{a in harm} softmax(s)_a, using the saved per-action outcome labels y in {-1,0,+1}. Train with the same softmax-and-threshold decision rule used at inference, so the threshold becomes part of training rather than a post-hoc calibration. This is the DeepMOT dustbin softmax made trainable. Change B (assignment surrogate, only if A shows signal): use the saved first-association inputs per frame (track and detection boxes, detection scores, baseline assignment; cache/native_cost_parity.json reports bit-exact cost parity on 128 rows). Build an expected cost row for each acting track: C_i(p) = p_0*C_i(baseline box) + sum_k p_k*C_i(box_k), where C = 1 - IoU*score as in fuse_score. Solve a log-domain Sinkhorn with a dustbin at cost 0.8, which mirrors lapjv with cost_limit = match_thresh, at temperature tau. Penalise the soft probability that each track is matched to a detection of a different GT identity, or loses its correct match: the analogue of dMOTA's FN~ + IDS~ including effects on neighbouring tracks. Use Sinkhorn or exact Hungarian with blackbox/perturbation gradients, not a learned DHN: DHN accuracy is about 93% and degrades with matrix size [S1 Table 5-6, Fig. 8]. Change C (GMTracker-inspired features): add target-neighbour relation inputs to the readout, e.g. the difference between FlyVis regional activity of the candidate region and of the competing track's best region, and pairwise relative geometry of candidate vs neighbours. This addresses explanation (2). Why this should fix a FlyVis problem: the measured failure is decision selection. Heads select 1,000-3,500 of 4,183 fit20 rows but only 13-33 change the outcome, the softmax probability never exceeds about 0.6, and many seeds abstain completely. That is what a regression-to-label objective that ignores the decision rule produces. Change A tests directly whether the FlyVis features carry the ranking information when trained for the decision. Equal controls, all with the identical loss, data, threshold rule and seeds: old D with the new loss vs old D with MSE (the existing z13_box_supervision_followup_v1 result, D vs baseline -0.06 pp [-0.24; +0.04]); stock FlyVis C; eye input R1 (pixels without FlyVis); no-fly geometry + context only. Per rule 6.16, a fly result requires D(new loss) > geometry-only(new loss) with a paired CI excluding 0. If geometry-only gains equally, the result is a tracker or readout-training improvement, not a FlyVis result. Cheap distinguishing check on saved data (CPU): (i) Train Change A heads on fit20+fit84 calibration rows with 3 seeds. Report on held-out videos the number of selected actions that change the outcome, beneficial minus harmful, at a threshold chosen on fit20, plus the mass on beneficial actions, for D, C, R1 and geometry-only. (ii) Replay HOTA offline on the 26 evaluation videos with the saved native association. Condition to proceed: D(new loss) beats both D(MSE) and geometry-only(new loss) in net beneficial corrections on held-out videos, with a bootstrap CI over videos excluding 0. The net gain should also correspond to a meaningful share of the full-box-in-eye reserve, e.g. at least 0.5 pp HOTA in replay before attempting the pre-registered +2 pp criterion [threshold to be fixed before the run]. Only then try Change B or C. A GPU stage is needed only if Change C requires new FlyVis maps (e.g. denser spatial activity than 68 regional features); nothing in these sources requires that.
strongest_objection: The method addresses a mismatch that our labels already mostly remove, while the measured bottleneck looks like missing discriminative information. Our good/neutral/harm labels are computed by replaying the native assignment with each action. So the only things a differentiable assignment adds are the decision rule in training and multi-track interactions. The saved calibrations show that the heads cannot rank the rare 13-33 outcome-changing actions above thousands of neutral ones at any threshold.
